# Conclusion

This perspective has argued that conformational gating is the operative selectivity mechanism in enzyme-mimetic metal-organic frameworks, and that framework flexibility is therefore a primary design variable rather than a defect to be minimised. Two actionable design rules follow from the analysis. First, linker flexibility should be tuned to position the gating free-energy barrier in the temperature and pH range relevant to the intended application: for ambient catalysis, a barrier of 15–20 kJ mol−1 appears optimal. Second, pore hydrophilicity — quantified by the PHI metric introduced here — should be matched to the coordination preference of the metal cofactor: high-PHI environments favour the high-affinity, high-coordination-number Ca2+ state, whereas low-PHI environments may be preferable for cofactors that operate in a lower coordination number regime.

The biological benchmarking data establish that these principles translate from isolated framework studies to the cellular context, lending confidence that the design rules have genuine predictive value beyond model systems. The clarity of the Ca2+ coordination switch in the MOF scaffold opens prospects for using these frameworks as structural model systems for mechanistic enzymology, independent of their catalytic utility. Together, the findings support a broader reorientation of biomimetic heterogeneous catalysis toward dynamic, flexibility-aware design — a direction that the community is well positioned to pursue given recent advances in flexible linker synthesis and in situ structural characterisation.
